newsitem.title: USA: Cohen to Congress: "Hemlock time" on defense.
newsitem.headline: Cohen to Congress: "Hemlock time" on defense.

text.p: U.S. Defense Secretary William Cohen warned on Friday that it was "hemlock time" for the tight military budget, urging a reluctant Congress to swallow political poison and close more military bases.
Cohen, who will unveil a new U.S. security and forces modernization proposal on Monday, told reporters that only very painful choices remained to save money for expensive new American weapons.

He said he had decided to recommend that Congress close more domestic bases instead of making deep cuts in the 1.4 million-member armed forces or cancelling costly fighter jet programs such as the F-18E/F and F-22 stealth fighters.

"These are the choices. There aren't any more easy ones. It's all hemlock time now," Cohen said in an interview in his office. "There are different flavors here. These are painful things that have got to be swallowed."

The secretary, who retired this year as a Republican senator from Maine, stressed that he had made unpopular choices in the review because "I am not running for anything -- I don't have to do the politically-correct thing anymore."

Military base closings are political dynamite because they mean billions of dollars in business and jobs to many U.S. communities. Congress has already approved four rounds of base closings in recent years.

Defense officials say privately that the Cohen proposal would cut only about 60,000 troops from active duty forces in order to keep the U.S. military stationed around the world and ready to fight two wars at once.
It will also seek cuts of about 75,000 in part-time reserve and National Guard forces.
The secretary predicted that there would be "fireworks" on Tuesday and Wednesday when he testifies to Congress on his recommendation to cut reserve forces and to close more domestic military bases.

"I will ultimately present them (Congress) with the choices I've had to make ... Do you want the bases or do you want the most modern equipment in the hands of the future fighting force of the country?"

Cohen said he had decided to reduce, but not cancel, the McDonnell Douglas Corp FA-18E/F and the Lockheed Martin Corp. F-22 "stealth" fighter programs and to also reduce numbers but speed delivery of the Marine Corps' MV-22 "tilt-rotor" helicopter to save money.
Defense officials said that planned purchases of the MV-22, built jointly by the Bell Helicopter division of Textron Inc and Boeing Co., would be reduced from 425 to 360.
The Air Force's previously planned purchase of 438 F-22s would be reduced to 339. The cost of that program under the full purchase had been estimated at about $67 billion.
Cohen will also recommend that Navy buys of the advanced FA-18E/F be cut to about 785, perhaps fewer. The Navy planned to buy 1,000 of the aircraft for about $80 billion by 2015.
The secretary told reporters that he had decided against killing the planned U.S. "Joint Strike Fighter" program which Lockheed Martin and Boeing Co. are competing to build in the next century.
Competition will be healthy between the F-18E/F and the Joint Strike Fighter, he said.

The winner of the Lockheed-Boeing competition is expected to eventually build as many as 3,000 of the fighters for more than $170 billion in the next century. Variations of the jet would go to the Air Force, Navy, Marines and British Royal Navy and could be sold to other countries.
